presentingComplaint: Progressive mid-back pain for 3 weeks with bilateral leg weakness and urinary hesitancy for 48 hours
history: Known metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason 8, diagnosed 2 years ago, on androgen-deprivation therapy). Three weeks of constant thoracic back pain, worse at night and on lying flat, unrelieved by paracetamol. Over the last 2 days he has noticed heaviness and weakness of both legs, unsteadiness when walking, a band-like tightness around the trunk, and difficulty initiating micturition with a sense of incomplete emptying. Reports numbness rising from the feet to just below the umbilicus. No trauma. No fever, no recent infection.
examination: Alert, oriented, not septic. Focal tenderness over the mid-thoracic spinous processes. Lower-limb power 3/5 bilaterally with increased tone, hyperreflexia at knees and ankles, bilateral upgoing plantars. Sensory level at approximately T10 to pinprick. Palpable bladder; reduced anal tone on PR with saddle sensory loss. Upper limbs and cranial nerves normal. Pertinent negatives: no neck stiffness, no meningism, no fever, no calf tenderness, no rash.
imaging: Urgent whole-spine MRI: T9-T10 posterior vertebral body metastasis with epidural soft-tissue extension causing thecal sac indentation and cord compression with early cord signal change; multiple sclerotic vertebral deposits. Bladder scan: 480 mL residual.
finalDiagnosis: Metastatic (malignant) spinal cord compression at T9-T10 from prostate carcinoma
citations: Harrison 22e — Approach to the Patient with Spinal Cord Disease / Neoplastic Diseases of the CNS
contraindications: Avoid delaying dexamethasone while awaiting imaging if MSCC strongly suspected
Screen for hyperglycaemia/PUD when starting high-dose steroids
Caution with NSAIDs given renal function and steroid co-use
edgeCases: Back pain can precede neurological signs by weeks — a normal neuro exam does not exclude impending MSCC
Autonomic (bladder/bowel) dysfunction and painless retention may be the only early sign; conus/cauda lesions give mixed UMN/LMN and saddle anaesthesia
Ambulatory status at treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome — treat as an emergency
expectedMaiK: This is a neuro-oncological emergency: back pain with a sensory level, bilateral leg weakness, hyperreflexia and new bladder dysfunction in a patient with known metastatic prostate cancer indicates malignant spinal cord compression. Give high-dose dexamethasone immediately and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI with oncology/neurosurgery review — do not wait.
expectedNextQuestions: Any bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness or reduced anal tone?
Is the pain worse on lying flat or at night, and is there a sensory level?
Is the patient still able to walk (ambulatory status)?
expectedInvestigations: Corrected calcium and baseline oncology bloods
